pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Reading Dinosaur Trackways (ages 7–9): use fossil footprints (trace fossils) to INFER a dinosaur's size, speed, and behaviour — bigger prints mean a bigger animal; widely spaced prints mean running, closely spaced mean walking; parallel trackways can mean animals moving together in a group.
• Standards — UK (DfE): 'working scientifically' (gathering and interpreting data, drawing conclusions from evidence); builds on the trace-fossil category.
• Standards — US (NGSS): grade-3 3-LS4-1 (interpret fossil evidence of organisms AND behaviour); an accessible instance of using data to infer.
• Operational details — This is a PROCEDURAL inference skill: measure a feature of the tracks, then reason to a conclusion. Print SIZE → body size; STRIDE (gap between prints) relative to print size → walking vs running (longer stride = faster); several PARALLEL trackways heading the same way → possible herd/group behaviour; two converging trackways → possible predator following prey. Stress that these are INFERENCES (well-supported guesses), not certainties, and that footprints capture a MOMENT of behaviour that bones cannot. Keep the reasoning qualitative (longer gap = faster) rather than the actual speed formula (that's later).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says bigger footprints mean a bigger dinosaur. Tier B (~8): uses print spacing to judge walking vs running. Tier C (~9): interprets a trackway scene (e.g. parallel tracks = group; converging = chase) and notes these are evidence-based inferences.
bestPractices: Frame every reading as 'measure a clue → make an inference', explicitly labelling conclusions as well-supported guesses.
Anchor speed to STRIDE RELATIVE TO SIZE (longer gap for its size = faster), not raw gap, to avoid a size confound.
Use whole-scene trackways (parallel, converging) so behaviour — herding, chasing — becomes readable, showing traces capture moments bones can't.
Contrast body-fossil evidence (what it looked like) with trace evidence (what it was doing) to reinforce why traces matter.
Invite alternative explanations (are parallel tracks really a herd, or just a popular path?) to model tentative reasoning.
keyRepresentations: A trackway map with measurable print size and stride spacing, plus a walk/run indicator.
Side-by-side trackways: closely spaced (walking) vs widely spaced (running).
A multi-trackway scene: parallel prints (group) and two converging sets (chase).
A 'clue → conclusion' annotation layer on the footprints.
commonMisconceptions: 'Footprints show what the dinosaur looked like' — they show behaviour/movement, not anatomy.
'Wider gaps always mean a bigger dinosaur' — gap indicates speed; size is shown by print size (must separate the two).
'A trackway proves a herd/chase' — these are plausible inferences, not certainties; other explanations exist.
'The deeper/larger print means it was running' — running is inferred from long stride relative to size, not depth alone.
'Footprints and the dinosaur's bones are always found together' — tracks are usually found without the track-maker's body.

learn.summary: Children aged 7–9 learn to read fossil dinosaur trackways (trace fossils) as evidence, using a 'measure a clue → make an inference' routine: print SIZE indicates approximate body size; STRIDE (the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot) relative to print size distinguishes walking (short stride for the print size) from running (long stride for the print size); several PARALLEL trackways in the same direction can suggest a group/herd; two CONVERGING trackways can suggest a predator following prey. Throughout, conclusions are framed as well-supported guesses, not certainties, and tracks are contrasted with body fossils to show that traces capture a moment of behaviour bones cannot. Core objective: separate the two variables — size is read from the print, speed from the spacing compared with print size — and keep reasoning qualitative (longer stride for its size = faster), not the numeric speed formula (that comes later).

activities.title: Palaeontologist's track-reading bench
feedback: If a learner calls the widely spaced prints 'the biggest dinosaur', separate the variables aloud: print size tells you approximate body size, the gap between prints compared with print size tells you speed — check each independently.

If a learner reads parallel tracks as one dinosaur pacing back and forth, have them count the distinct trackways and note they run parallel in the same direction — a pattern consistent with several animals moving together, though they could also have passed at different times.
If a learner says 'they're just marks, you can't tell anything', model one inference aloud (a short stride for the size of the print suggests walking) then hand the next track back for them to try.
If a learner judges speed from how deep or large a print is, note that running is inferred from a long stride relative to print size, not from depth alone.
Affirm tentative language: praise a learner who says a chase or herd is 'likely' and can name an alternative explanation.
activities.rationale: The skill is procedural, so learners should carry out the measure-and-reason loop themselves. Making stride adjustable against a fixed print size directly targets the common size/speed confound, and a scene with parallel and converging tracks makes herding and chasing readable while the alternative-explanation prompt models tentative reasoning.
sourceClaims: Trackways allow inferences about the track-maker: footprint size scales with body size; stride length relative to size distinguishes walking from running; parallel trackways can indicate gregarious/herd behaviour and converging tracks possible predator-prey interactions — all interpreted as evidence-based inferences.
learnerActions: Measure a single large footprint and read off an approximate, tentative body-size estimate it suggests (e.g. 'about as tall as a house'), treating that figure as a rough guide that depends on the species rather than a certainty.
Measure the stride in a trackway: the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot.

For a fixed print size, lengthen the stride and watch a gait indicator swing from WALK toward RUN, so that speed is read from the SPACING compared with print size while size is read from the PRINT — two separate questions.

In a whole-scene mode, interpret multiple trackways: tag parallel sets as a possible herd travelling together, and two converging sets as a possible predator trailing prey, attaching your inference and how confident you are.
Respond to a 'could it be something else?' prompt by proposing an alternative explanation (e.g. parallel tracks might just be a popular path, not a herd).

Predict what the dinosaurs were doing, then watch one possible reconstruction animate them walking, running, and moving together as the tracks suggest, and compare it with your prediction, remembering the animation is an interpretation, not a recording.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading trackways is a measure-then-infer procedure: print size answers how big, stride compared with print size answers how fast, scene patterns suggest behaviour, and every conclusion is an evidence-based inference rather than a certainty.

activities.title: Annotated trackway scene: tap to reveal the reasoning
feedback: When an annotation is revealed, ask the learner to restate the clue and the conclusion in their own words before moving on.
If the reveal surprises them, revisit which measurement (print size or stride) drove that conclusion.
activities.rationale: An annotated reveal clearly conveys the clue→conclusion structure and is a useful scaffold, but because the learner cannot vary spacing or arrange the scene, it shows the procedure rather than letting them practise it — best used before or alongside the hands-on bench.
learnerActions: Study a trackway scene and, before revealing, state what each print's size and spacing suggest.
Tap individual prints to reveal size → body-size and spacing → gait annotations, checking them against your own reading.
Tap a multi-track scene to reveal the herd and chase interpretations, then say why those are plausible rather than certain.
activities.intendedInsight: The clue→conclusion links (size→body, spacing→gait, pattern→behaviour) can be made explicit and checked, reinforcing what each measurement supports.

activities.title: Check your reading: compare and interpret trackways
feedback: If a learner picks the trackway with the biggest prints as the 'running' one, point them back to stride length relative to size, not print size.
For 'what might parallel tracks mean?', accept a herd answer but prompt for at least one alternative to keep the conclusion tentative.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and slider items assess the target inferences efficiently and make a good checkpoint, but on their own they test recognition rather than building the hands-on measure-and-reason loop, so pair them with a constructive activity.
learnerActions: Given two trackways drawn to the same scale, decide which shows running and justify it from stride relative to print size.
Interpret a multi-track scene by choosing what parallel tracks might mean and what two converging sets might mean.
Use a slider to estimate 'how big was the maker?' from print size alone, keeping it separate from the speed judgement.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can demonstrate that they read size from the print and speed from the spacing, and can offer plausible behavioural interpretations as inferences.

activities.title: Explain-your-thinking with a curious expert
feedback: If the learner asserts a conclusion without evidence, ask which specific measurement supports it before accepting it.
If the learner treats a very deep print as proof of running, note that depth may reflect ground softness or weight, while running is inferred from long stride relative to size.
Reward answers that acknowledge uncertainty and name an alternative explanation.
activities.rationale: Socratic probing fits the tentative-inference theme and surfaces reasoning, especially on novel tracks (crossing, deep prints). It complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on measuring that most directly delivers the measure-and-infer skill at this age.
learnerActions: Present your reading of a trackway and answer probing questions such as 'How do you know it was running?' and 'Could parallel tracks mean something other than a herd?'

Work through novel cases aloud: if two trackways cross, reason about which dinosaur passed first; compare what very deep prints versus shallow prints in the same ground might tell you; decide whether a small dinosaur could ever leave widely spaced prints and when.
Revise a claim when you cannot justify it, distinguishing a well-supported inference from a guess.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying each reading out loud and handling novel tracks strengthens the habit of treating conclusions as tentative, evidence-based inferences.

activities.title: Explore a 3D trackway site in situ (alternative)
feedback: If the learner judges speed from print size or depth, redirect them to stride length relative to print size.
Encourage the learner to name at least one alternative explanation before settling on a herd or chase reading.
activities.rationale: Exploring tracks in situ may add immersion and a sense of real scale. Whether the extra navigation helps or hinders the core 2D measuring reasoning is a design consideration rather than an established fact, so this is offered as an untested alternative to the flat bench, not a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Move through a preserved three-dimensional trackway and locate a continuous line of prints.
Measure a print's size and the stride between prints in place, reading an approximate, tentative body size from the print and gait from the stride relative to size.
Interpret whether nearby parallel or converging trackways might suggest a group or a chase, framing each as a possible inference and naming an alternative.
Compare how examining tracks in a 3D setting feels against reading them on a flat bench.
activities.intendedInsight: The same measure→infer reasoning (size→body, stride→gait, pattern→behaviour) applies when tracks are examined in a three-dimensional, in-situ setting.

constraints: Keep reasoning qualitative (longer stride for its size = faster); do not introduce the numeric speed formula at this age.
Anchor speed to stride RELATIVE TO print size, not raw gap, to avoid confusing size and speed.
Always frame herd, chase, and predator-prey readings as plausible inferences with possible alternatives, never as proven facts.
Treat body-size readouts (e.g. 'as tall as a house') as approximate, species-dependent estimates, not exact measurements.
Running is inferred from long stride relative to print size, not from print depth or size alone; depth can reflect ground softness or weight.

Reveal-only annotated scenes and selected-response/slider checks are scaffolds or assessments: they show or test the inference but do not let the learner vary spacing or arrange a scene, so they do not by themselves build the constructive measure-and-reason skill; this is their observable limit, not a claim that any medium is universally superior.
Tracks are usually found without the track-maker's body; use this to contrast trace evidence (what it was doing) with body-fossil evidence (what it looked like).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false and was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim is attributed to Natural History Museum (UK)/USGS education resources but is unverified; treat the quantitative-sounding relationships (size↔body, stride↔gait) as qualitative teaching heuristics, not precise measurements.

A '3D trackway site' option from the legacy notes carried a categorical claim that '3D adds navigation cost without improving the inference'. That is a design preference, not an established fact, so it has been retained as a qualified alternative activity with proposed/may wording rather than deleted or asserted.

The 'about as tall as a house' body-size readout is an illustrative, approximate mapping; actual size inferences from prints depend on species and are uncertain, so such readouts are kept clearly tentative in the activity itself.

sourceClaims were narrowed to [] on the annotated-reveal, selected-response/slider, conversation, and 3D activities because their rationales concern the delivery medium (scaffold, assessment, Socratic probing, immersion), which the single source claim about trackway inferences does not directly support; the source is retained only where the rationale invokes the actual inference relationships.

probeDeeper: If two trackways cross each other, how would you work out which dinosaur passed by first?
What would very deep prints tell you compared with shallow ones in the same ground?
Could a small dinosaur ever leave prints spaced far apart? When would that happen?
assess.correctAnswer: Track A: a small dinosaur, walking (small prints, short stride). Track B: a large dinosaur, running (large prints, long stride between them). Track C: several dinosaurs travelling together as a group (parallel tracks, same direction). Print SIZE indicates body size; the GAP between prints indicates speed; PARALLEL tracks indicate a herd.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates stride with size: 'the far-apart prints mean the biggest dinosaur.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two variables explicitly — print size tells you body size, the gap between prints tells you speed; check each independently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels Track B the biggest because the prints are spread out, ignoring the actual print size.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads parallel trackways as one busy animal rather than several: 'it's one dinosaur that walked back and forth.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the distinct trackways and note they run parallel in the same direction and spacing — a signature of animals travelling together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts Track C as a single pacing dinosaur instead of a group moving together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies any inference is possible: 'they're just marks, you can't tell anything.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model one inference aloud (short stride = walking) then hand the next track back for the child to try.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to reason from the prints, treating them as decoration rather than evidence.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the pictures literally with no measurement — e.g. calls the spread-out prints 'the biggest' and makes no size/speed distinction.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates print size, stride spacing and track pattern together to reconstruct size, gait and social behaviour, and reasons sensibly about a novel track such as crossing or deep prints.
responseLevels.partial: Makes single, isolated inferences (big prints mean a big dinosaur) but does not combine spacing to judge speed or read parallel tracks as a group.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three trackways drawn to the same scale. Track A: small prints spaced close together. Track B: large prints spaced far apart. Track C: several sets of prints side by side, all heading the same way. For each track, work out what it tells you about the dinosaur — how big it was, whether it was walking or running, and whether it was alone or in a group. Talk me through your reasoning as you go.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can perform the reading measures print size and stride separately and links stride length to speed. A child who cannot guesses from the overall picture or reads body size off the spacing, conflating the two variables.

sources.claim: Trackways allow inferences about the track-maker: footprint size scales with body size; stride length relative to size distinguishes walking from running; parallel trackways can indicate gregarious/herd behaviour and converging tracks possible predator-prey interactions — all interpreted as evidence-based inferences.
